_what: WHAT A THING IS, declared rather than read off a name. Four classifications the read service applies to every response. Each was a string test in service/queries.py until 2026-09-09; each was correct when written and wrong the day a store or a league was named differently. RS-G8 derives all three from the model and lists every difference.
_why: Three of the same defect in one file. `store.startswith("stats-")` called PFA's 2,688,935 statistics ordinary facts because its stores are named pfa-stats-1920s..2020s. `league NOT IN ('COACHES','ASSISTANTS','SALARIES','COACH')` called 41,662 coaching claims playing claims the day the coaching subjects were given real leagues. `predicate not in ("name",)` served pfa.name_as_printed twice and left statscrew.formal_name unsearchable. A rule that reads a VALUE where it should read a DECLARATION is right until someone names the next thing differently.
_gate: service/gates.py RS-G8. It does not trust this file: it re-derives each classification from the model and fails on any difference, in both directions.

statistic_stores._what: The stores whose stint claims are per-season STATISTICS -- they belong in the `statistics` block of a stint, not in `facts`. Named one by one on purpose: a prefix rule is what broke this.
statistic_stores._measured_2026_09_09: 228 stores, 4,589,438 claims, every one stint-scoped. The predicate sets are DISJOINT: 171 predicates appear in these stores and 184 elsewhere, and NOT ONE appears in both. That disjointness is what RS-G8 checks, so a store added here that carries a roster predicate fails, and a statistics store left out fails.
statistic_stores._two_naming_conventions_not_one: `stats-<league>-<year>` (217) came from StatsCrew and is paired one-to-one with a roster store of the same name minus the prefix -- that pairing is a SEPARATE rule and lives in build_person_index.py and league_tokens.py, which strip the prefix to find the roster store. `pfa-stats-<decade>` (11) came from PFA on 2026-09-08 and has NO paired roster store. Neither of those two files should read this declaration: they are asking which roster store a local id belongs to, not what the claims mean.

staff_predicates._moved_2026_09_09: This section now lives in dataset/declarations/coaching-seasons.json. It is the ARCHIVE's ruling: src/build_person_index.py sorts the person index by the same list, and two copies of one rule is the defect this whole file exists to prevent. service/classification.py reads it from there.

name_predicates._what: Person-scoped predicates whose value is a man's NAME. They are served under `names`, indexed for search, and kept OUT of `facts` -- a name is not a fact about a man, it is how a source wrote him.
name_predicates._history: queries.py excluded the single literal "name", so pfa.name_as_printed was served twice (it IS read into person_name by the builder) and statscrew.formal_name and full_name were served as facts only -- 1,607 name claims that search_people could not find.
name_predicates._club_name_is_not_here: `club_name` is club_season-scoped and names a CLUB. Scope is part of the test.

_shapes.name: a plain string.
_shapes.pfa.name_as_printed: a dict, not a string -- the builder already reads it into person_name and takes the printed form out of it. Kept here so the two readers agree on what a name is.
_shapes.statscrew.formal_name: a plain string; the full formal name where StatsCrew prints one.
_shapes.pfr.full_name: Pro-Football-Reference's full name from a player page -- 'Clarence Edward Horning' where the archive holds 'Steamer Horning'. A NAME, added 2026-09-09 when RS-G8 caught it sitting in `facts` where search could not find it.
_shapes.wikipedia.full_name: the same, from a Wikipedia article. It is the whole point of the Plunkett ingest: the archive held him as `Plunkett` and this is his forename.

name_predicates._added_2026_09_09: fyjbook.name_as_printed -- the Frankford book site prints the full formal name with the nickname inside where the archive holds the short form (`Doc Elliott` against `Wallace "Doc" Elliott`). Ryan's ruling: these go in BESIDE what is held, not over it, and both stay searchable. A name that is not a declared name predicate is served as a fact and never indexed, which is how 1,607 names became unsearchable once before.

name_forms._what: WHICH FORM A NAME IS WRITTEN IN. Surname-first (`Pollard, Frederick Douglass`) is a FILING CONVENTION, not a name as anyone reads it. Ruled 2026-09-09 by Ryan: where a person holds both forms, the derived display name takes the forename-first one. NOTHING IS STANDARDISED -- both stay as printed in the store, both stay name claims, both stay searchable. This decides only which one the §9.3 recipe is allowed to choose from.
name_forms._why_the_string_and_not_the_predicate: Measured 2026-09-09 on the whole index: the form does NOT follow the predicate. `name` carries 612 comma forms out of 174,339 (Crippen's register: `ZORICH, George`); `statscrew.formal_name` is only 6% comma (101 of 1,586) -- most StatsCrew formal names are already forename-first, so declaring that predicate 'the surname-first one' would be wrong 94% of the time; `pfa.name_as_printed` is 50%, because it carries two forms in one value. No source files consistently, so no declaration of SOURCES can decide it. The form is a property of the string, and reading a value to learn something about that value is a READING, which the archive applies at read time and never writes back.
name_forms._the_rule: Split on the FIRST comma. Set aside, in the tail, any parenthetical and any generational suffix. If anything remains, the head was a surname standing alone and the name is SURNAME-FIRST. If nothing remains, the comma was only introducing a suffix and the name is forename-first.
name_forms._why_a_bare_comma_test_is_wrong: 2,472 index names carry a comma. 110 of them are `Forename Surname, Jr.` -- forename-first with a suffix -- and 170 carry more than one comma, including `Grantis D. Bell, Jr., Jr., Jr.` (forename-first, a source repeating itself) and `ALFORD, Herbert Bruce, Sr. (Bruce)` (surname-first WITH a suffix and a nickname). A test on the comma alone gets both wrong.
name_forms._what_it_cannot_tell: `Smith, Jones` -- two surnames, or a surname and a forename that is also a surname -- reads as surname-first. So does any two-part name whose second part is not a suffix. The rule cannot see the difference and does not pretend to; it is stated here so a reader knows the limit rather than discovering it.
name_forms._measured_2026_09_09: 2,405 people hold both forms and 12 hold only a surname-first form. A person holding only surname-first KEEPS it -- the ruling is a preference between forms held, never the deletion of the only name a man has.

worked_examples._what: Every one of these is a real string in the index, with the answer the reading MUST give. RS-G8 checks them, so editing the suffix list or the rule fails loudly instead of silently re-sorting names. Both answers are represented: a rule tested only on the cases it is meant to catch is tested on nothing.
forename_first: Grantis D. Bell, Jr., Jr., Jr.
worked_examples._bare_surname: Pairs the bare-surname rule must decide, checked by RS-G8. Each is (the one-word name, the names held beside it, whether it is set aside).

a_bare_surname_is_not_preferred._what: Ruled by Ryan, 2026-09-09. Where a person holds a name of ONE WORD and also a longer name ENDING IN THAT WORD, the one-word name is set aside as a display-name candidate. A display name exists to be read; a bare surname is what survives when nothing else does, not a name to prefer over a fuller one for the same man.
a_bare_surname_is_not_preferred._the_defect: P_002634 held `Plunkett` from a dated 1920 roster and `Joseph T. Plunkett` from an undated Wikipedia article. The 9.3 recipe prefers the name covering the largest attested span and an undated claim counts toward none, so the archive knew his forename and showed a surname.
a_bare_surname_is_not_preferred._the_rule_exactly: A candidate is set aside when (a) it is a single word after splitting on whitespace, and (b) another candidate has two or more words whose LAST word equals it, compared case-insensitively and ignoring a trailing full stop or comma. Nothing else.

_how_far_it_reaches_MEASURED_2026_09_09._the_other_one: P_011767 Breaux already displays `Delvin Breaux`: his fuller name is DATED, so the span rule reaches it without help. The rule confirms him rather than moving him.

a_bare_surname_is_not_preferred._what_this_ruling_does_NOT_decide: Which of two MULTI-WORD names is fuller. `Joseph T. Plunkett` against `Joe Plunkett` is a different question and is left open, exactly as ruled.
a_bare_surname_is_not_preferred._the_wider_rule_that_was_rejected: A containment rule -- every word of A appears in B and B is longer -- reaches 1,616 people and is WRONG twice over. It would prefer a middle name nobody uses (`Anthony Amos` -> `Anthony Tyrone Amos, II`), and it would fight the surname-first ruling by preferring `Moore, Sterling Patrick` over `Sterling Moore`. Measured before choosing, not assumed.
a_bare_surname_is_not_preferred._it_is_a_filter_not_a_new_recipe: Like the surname-first rule beside it, this removes candidates and then the 9.3 span rule runs unchanged. A man who holds NOTHING but a bare surname keeps it: the filters never empty the set.
